# Block 6: Writing figure legends {.unnumbered}


```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(ggdist)
library(colorspace)

# Data and statistics for the legend repair challenge, computed here so the
# numbers in the model answer always match the figure
legend_data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(body_mass_g)
n_sp <- dplyr::count(legend_data, species)
n_of <- function(sp) n_sp$n[n_sp$species == sp]
legend_fit <- anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = legend_data))
legend_F   <- round(legend_fit$`F value`[1], 1)
legend_df1 <- legend_fit$Df[1]
legend_df2 <- legend_fit$Df[2]
```

A figure in a journal or lab report is not finished until its legend is. The legend lets a reader understand the figure without going back to the main text, which is the third of the three questions for every figure (Block 7): *is the figure self-contained?*

## The four elements

Write a legend as four elements, in this order:

1. **Descriptive sentence.** What the figure shows, stated neutrally, in the past tense. A description, not a result.
2. **Methods and sample.** Where the data came from (with a citation), the sample size for each group, and any exclusions.
3. **Statistical model and result.** The test, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, the p-value (exact, or bounded such as p < 0.001), and any adjustment for multiple comparisons. Leave this element out if the figure is purely descriptive: never invent a test to fill it.
4. **Visual components defined.** Every layer on the figure (density, box, points, error bars, colours, shapes) explained.

Most bad legends fail in one of two ways: they are too vague (leaving out details the reader needs), or they put the wrong kind of thing in an element (a result where a description belongs, or a plot name where a definition belongs).

## Game: legend triage

The facilitator puts each fragment on screen. Post your verdict in the chat, then check it here.

| Fragment | Your verdict |
|---|---|
| "Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica." | `r mcq(c(answer = "Good", "Bad: a result, not a description", "Bad: too vague or missing details", "Bad: names the plot but defines nothing"))` |
| "Gentoo penguins are heavier." | `r mcq(c("Good", answer = "Bad: a result, not a description", "Bad: too vague or missing details", "Bad: names the plot but defines nothing"))` |
| "n = 342." | `r mcq(c("Good", "Bad: a result, not a description", answer = "Bad: too vague or missing details", "Bad: names the plot but defines nothing"))` |
| "Shows a raincloud plot." | `r mcq(c("Good", "Bad: a result, not a description", "Bad: too vague or missing details", answer = "Bad: names the plot but defines nothing"))` |
| "ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05)." | `r mcq(c("Good", "Bad: a result, not a description", answer = "Bad: too vague or missing details", "Bad: names the plot but defines nothing"))` |

`r hide("Why?")`

- **"n = 342"** gives only the total. The reader needs the sample size for each group, the data source and any exclusions.
- **"ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05)"** names a test, but gives no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and only a threshold rather than the p-value.
- **"Shows a raincloud plot"** tells the reader what kind of plot it is, but not what the cloud, the box or the points mean.

`r unhide()`

## 🏆 Challenge: legend repair

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
legend_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.06, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

> **Figure 1.** Gentoo penguins are heavier. Data from a survey (n = 342). Species differed significantly (p < 0.05). Shows a raincloud plot.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Legend repair (solo race, 10 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

The legend above breaks every rule. Rewrite it as a four-element legend for this figure.

What you need to know:

- The data are body masses from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020). Penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded.
- A one-way ANOVA of body mass on species was fitted, with Tukey-adjusted pairwise contrasts.
- Work out the sample sizes and the ANOVA result yourself:

```{r}
#| eval: false
legend_data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(body_mass_g)

count(legend_data, species)

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = legend_data))
```

Post your legend in the chat. **Scoring:** one point for each element that is present and correct, and a bonus point if every visual layer (cloud, box, points) is defined. The facilitator reads out the best one.

::::
:::

`r hide("Solution: a four-element legend")`

> **Figure 1.** Body mass (g) of three penguin species (*Pygoscelis adeliae*, *P. antarcticus* and *P. papua*) in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Data are from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020); penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded, giving `r n_of("Adelie")` Adelie, `r n_of("Chinstrap")` Chinstrap and `r n_of("Gentoo")` Gentoo individuals. A one-way ANOVA showed that body mass differed between species (F(`r legend_df1`, `r legend_df2`) = `r legend_F`, p < 0.001); pairwise contrasts were Tukey-adjusted. The shaded region shows a kernel density estimate of each distribution; the box shows the interquartile range with the median as a horizontal line; points are individual penguins, jittered horizontally.

The four elements are, in order: the descriptive sentence; the source, exclusions and sample sizes; the test and its result; and the definitions of the cloud, box and points. Note that the legend still *describes*: the conclusion ("Gentoo are heavier") belongs in the main text or, for a talk or poster, in an explanatory title (Block 2).

`r unhide()`

:::{.callout-note}
In the Quarto session you will put a legend like this into a figure's `fig-cap` option, so the caption travels with the figure and can be cross-referenced in your text.
:::

## Block 7: Three questions for every figure

Every figure you produce, in every context, should answer three questions. If it cannot, it is not finished.

1. **Does the visual impression match the data?** Honest axes, appropriate encoding, no distortion. The reader should reach the same conclusion from the figure that they would reach from the underlying numbers.

2. **Who is the audience and does the design serve them?** Complexity, annotation density, and font size calibrated to the reader. A journal figure, a poster figure and a public engagement figure each need a different design.

3. **Is the figure self-contained?** Labels, units, a legend that defines every visual layer, and ideally the script that produced it, so a future reader (including yourself) can reconstruct what you did and why.

**Final check: true or false?**

- A bar chart of means may start its y-axis at any value, as long as it is labelled. `r torf(FALSE)`
- Colour should never be the only cue that distinguishes groups. `r torf(TRUE)`
- `theme_barbie()` is fine for a journal figure if the reviewers like pink. `r torf(FALSE)`
- An interactive `ggiraph` figure can replace the static figure in a PDF manuscript. `r torf(FALSE)`
- Setting `base_size` scales every text element in the figure together. `r torf(TRUE)`
- A figure legend should state the main conclusion in its first sentence. `r torf(FALSE)`

## Take-home exercise

Your homework is to apply everything from the workshop to your own data. The aim is to produce one publication-ready figure from your own dataset, using the techniques from Blocks 1 to 7.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Take-home: one publication-ready figure
::::
::::{.task-container}
Choose a dataset from your own research with at least one continuous variable, one categorical grouping, and a sample size of at least thirty observations. Produce one publication-ready figure that applies the principles and extensions from this workshop:

1. **Block 1.** Variable types determine the chart. Honest axes. Accessible palette via `colorspace`. The encoding hierarchy applied: most important variable to position, most important categorical to colour hue with shape redundantly.
2. **Block 2.** Audience-appropriate framing: pick journal/lab report unless you have a specific other audience in mind. Descriptive title.
3. **Block 3.** A `theme_project()` (or equivalent) applied; scales formatted with `scales::breaks_pretty()` and an appropriate `scales::label_*()` function for the units.
4. **Block 4.** At least one extension used appropriately (raincloud distribution display, direct labelling with `ggrepel` or `ggtext`, or multi-panel composition with `patchwork`).
5. **Block 5.** Save the figure as both PDF and PNG using `ragg::agg_png` for the PNG; verify with `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` before saving.
6. **Block 6.** Write a four-element legend for it.
7. **Block 7.** Check it against the three questions.
::::
:::


### A skeleton to adapt

```{r}
#| eval: false
# !! PARTICIPANT: replace the data load with your own file.
my_data <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "my_data.csv"))

# Source the project theme function defined in Block 3
# (paste theme_project() into R/functions/plot_functions.R first)
source(here::here("R", "functions", "plot_functions.R"))

# Build the figure using the patterns from Blocks 1-4.
# Example structure (modify to match your variables and audience):
my_figure <- my_data |>
  tidyr::drop_na(<your_continuous_var>, <your_grouping_var>) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = <your_grouping_var>,
                               y = <your_continuous_var>,
                               fill = <your_grouping_var>)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 6)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "<Variable name (unit)>") +
  theme_project(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

# Verify accessibility before saving
colorBlindness::cvdPlot(my_figure)

# Save in both formats
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.pdf"),
  plot = my_figure,
  width = 7, height = 5, units = "in"
)
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.png"),
  plot = my_figure,
  width = 7, height = 5, units = "in",
  dpi = 300, device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white"
)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
If your figure passes `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` and the legend would let someone understand it without the manuscript text, you have met the standard. If either fails, fix it before submitting.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
**These rules as an AI skill.** Everything in this workshop, from the chart-type and audience tables to the accessibility check and the two-format save, can be written down once for an AI assistant to follow. Day 4 does exactly that: the [instructions-and-skills block](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) provides `pub-figures`, a skill that packages these conventions with a fuller version of `theme_project()`, and shows you how to test whether an assistant actually follows them.
:::
